summary: The kings of England held the Duchy of Aquitaine (Gascony) as vassals of the French crown, a long source of friction. When Philip VI confiscated it in 1337, Edward III answered by claiming the French throne through his mother. The war that followed was a series of campaigns broken by long truces. In the Edwardian phase England won at Sluys, Crécy and Poitiers, captured King John II and gained an enlarged Aquitaine at Brétigny in 1360. Under Charles V the French recovered almost everything. Henry V reopened the war, won at Agincourt in 1415, conquered Normandy and, allied with Burgundy during a French civil war, was named heir to France by the Treaty of Troyes. Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans in 1429 and Burgundy's return to the French side in 1435 turned the tide; with better artillery and a professional army, France took Normandy and Gascony, leaving England only Calais after Castillon in 1453.
casualties: Estimates are very uncertain: one widely repeated compilation counts about 185,000 soldiers killed in battle and some 556,000 military deaths in all, while raiding, famine and the Black Death killed far more civilians, especially in France.

brief.hook: English kings ruled Gascony as vassals of the French crown; when Philip VI seized it in 1337, Edward III claimed the throne of France itself.

sides.who: The Kingdom of England with English Gascony, Welsh archers and, from 1419 to 1435, the Duchy of Burgundy
The Kingdom of France, with its old ally Scotland and, from 1369, the Crown of Castile and its fleet

brief.resultLine: After the French beat the English at Castillon on 17 July 1453, Bordeaux surrendered on 19 October; no peace was signed, but England kept only Calais.

strategies.name: Longbows and the chevauchée
strategies.text: English armies were mostly longbowmen, who shot down charging French knights at Crécy and Agincourt. Between battles, mounted raids called chevauchées burned French towns and farms to ruin the king's revenue.

strategies.name: Avoiding battle
strategies.text: Charles V and his constable du Guesclin refused pitched battles. They let English raids pass, picked off foragers and retook the lands lost at Brétigny town by town in the 1370s.

strategies.name: Guns and a standing army
strategies.text: In 1445 Charles VII set up a permanent paid army, and Jean Bureau built a powerful artillery train. Its guns helped retake Normandy and broke Talbot's attack at Castillon in 1453.

impact: England lost all its lands in France except Calais, which it held until 1558.
France built one of the first standing armies in Western Europe since Roman times, and gunpowder artillery proved its worth.
Defeat left the English crown deep in debt, and quarrels among its nobles fed the Wars of the Roses from 1455.

details: Edward III held Gascony, the remnant of the Duchy of Aquitaine, as a vassal of the French king, and the French crown had long sought to assert its sovereignty there. In May 1337 Philip VI's Great Council declared the duchy forfeit, citing Edward's breach of his duties as vassal and his shelter of Philip's enemy Robert of Artois. Edward replied by reviving his claim to the French throne through his mother Isabella, sister of the last Capetian king.

The cloth towns of Flanders depended on English wool, and Edward courted them and other Low Countries princes as allies. On 26 January 1340 he received homage as king of France from Guy, half-brother of the count of Flanders, and the civic authorities of Ghent, Ypres and Bruges proclaimed him their king. Adopting the French title let his Flemish supporters claim they were loyal to the true king of France rather than rebels against their overlord.

Edward sailed from England with a fleet of some 120–150 ships and found the much larger French fleet drawn up in defensive formation in the inlet off Sluys in Flanders. Attacking in the afternoon with the wind and sun behind them, the English almost destroyed the French fleet. England dominated the Channel for the rest of the war, which kept the fighting on French soil and made a French invasion of England impractical.

With Edward's money running out, the war might have ended, but the death of the duke of Brittany in 1341 started a succession dispute between John of Montfort and Charles of Blois, nephew of Philip VI. Edward backed Montfort and Philip backed Blois, and for years the war centred on Brittany, where towns such as Vannes changed hands several times. The English-backed Montfort finally won the duchy in 1364.

Edward landed at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue on the Cotentin peninsula with complete surprise and marched south, his soldiers razing towns and looting as they went. The army captured the rich city of Caen in a single day, then turned north-east, pillaging toward the Low Countries. Finding the Seine bridges destroyed, Edward crossed at Poissy near Paris and then forded the Somme at Blanchetaque, slipping away from Philip's pursuing army.

Unable to outmarch Philip VI, Edward chose a defensive position near Crécy. Genoese mercenary crossbowmen were driven back in an archery duel by English and Welsh longbowmen, and the French knights then launched a series of disordered cavalry charges into arrow fire and dismounted men-at-arms. The French suffered heavy losses, including many nobles, and Philip had allowed the attack to begin before his army was ready.

Scotland had been bound to France by the Auld Alliance since 1295. Philip appealed to the Scots to relieve the pressure by invading northern England, and King David II led an army south. Near Durham, at Neville's Cross, it was defeated and David himself was captured. The defeat greatly reduced the Scottish threat to England for the following years and freed Edward to continue his campaign in France.

After Crécy, Edward marched north unopposed and besieged the Channel port of Calais, which held out until it surrendered in 1347. The town became England's main base in France, letting it land and supply troops safely in the north. Calais stayed English long after the war ended, until the French retook it in 1558. Together with Crécy and Neville's Cross, its capture capped a run of English successes in 1346–1347.

The plague pandemic that swept Europe arrived in Paris in 1348 and killed a very large share of the population of both kingdoms; estimates for France run to 6–12 million deaths, 30–60 percent of the population, and for England 2–3 million. Fighting was largely suspended while the epidemic raged. The losses strained recruitment and royal finances on both sides, and English campaigning on a large scale resumed only in 1355.

Edward III's eldest son, Edward of Woodstock, later called the Black Prince, led a chevauchée, a mounted raid designed to ruin the enemy's lands and revenue, from Bordeaux across southern France. His army pillaged Avignonet, Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Narbonne. Such raids, repeated throughout the war, burned towns and crops and fell hardest on the peasants of France rather than on its armies.

On a second raid the Black Prince was overtaken near Poitiers by King John II. The French, some 14,000–16,000 strong, attacked about 6,000 Anglo-Gascons in a strong defensive position. A mounted force led by the Gascon captal de Buch, hidden in a wood, struck their flank and cut off their retreat, and John and many nobles were captured. With the king a prisoner, his son the Dauphin Charles ruled as regent amid growing disorder.

Edward invaded France a third time, hoping to be crowned at Reims, but the city held out for five weeks, and the Dauphin refused battle. After skirmishes outside Paris the English moved toward Chartres, where a freak hailstorm struck their camp at Easter and killed more than 1,000 men. The disaster pushed Edward to negotiate when the French approached him.

Drafted at Brétigny near Chartres and ratified at Calais in October, the treaty gave Edward full sovereignty over a much larger Aquitaine, including Gascony, Poitou, Saintonge, Limousin and other lands, plus Calais and Ponthieu. In return he gave up Normandy, Touraine, Anjou and Maine and his claim to the French crown. John II's ransom was set at three million écus, with hostages held as guarantee.

In Castile's civil war the Black Prince restored Peter of Castile by winning the battle of Nájera, but the campaign left him in debt. His new hearth tax in Aquitaine provoked Gascon lords to appeal to Charles V, who summoned the prince to Paris; the prince refused, and war broke out again in 1369. That year Henry of Trastámara, backed by France, killed Peter, and Castile became an important French naval ally.

Castile's new Trastámara regime repaid French support with naval help. In 1372 a Castilian fleet defeated an English fleet off La Rochelle, an important port in western France. The defeat weakened English control of the sea routes to Aquitaine, and under the cautious strategy of Charles V and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin, who avoided pitched battles, the French steadily took back English-held towns.

Charles V's small professional army under du Guesclin had pushed the English back so far that when the king died in 1380, the vast lands won at Brétigny had shrunk to Calais and a few coastal towns. The Black Prince had died in 1376 and Edward III in 1377, and England, ruled for the boy king Richard II, faced heavy war taxation and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

With the war unpopular in England and neither side able to pay for major campaigns, negotiations led to the three-year Truce of Leulinghem, signed on 18 June 1389. Renewed several times, it brought a long lull. In the following decades Charles VI of France suffered bouts of madness, and the rivalry of the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans turned into civil war between Burgundians and Armagnacs, both of which sought English help.

Henry V landed in August 1415 and took Harfleur after a long siege. Marching toward Calais with a tired, hungry army, he was forced to fight a much larger French army near Agincourt. English archers and men-at-arms on a narrow, muddy field inflicted catastrophic losses, killing many leaders of the Armagnac faction. Fearing an attack, Henry ordered most of the French prisoners, perhaps thousands, to be killed.

Henry conquered Normandy, taking Caen in 1417 and Rouen in January 1419. Meanwhile the Burgundians had seized Paris in 1418. On 10 September 1419 Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy was killed by one of the Dauphin Charles's attendants during a meeting on the bridge at Montereau, and his son Philip the Good allied formally with England. The Anglo-Burgundian alliance gave Henry control of Paris and much of northern France.

Sealed at Troyes with the insane Charles VI, the treaty disinherited the Dauphin Charles and named Henry and his heirs successors to the French crown. Charles VI remained king for life, and Henry married his daughter Catherine of Valois. Henry entered Paris later that year. The Dauphin, holding much of France south of the Loire, rejected the treaty, so the war became a contest between two claimants.

Henry V died in August 1422, two months before Charles VI, leaving a baby son, Henry VI, as king of England and, by the treaty, of France. His brother the Duke of Bedford ran English France. At Verneuil in Normandy, Bedford's archers devastated a Franco-Scottish army, virtually destroying the Dauphin's field army and ending the Scots' role as a major force in France for the rest of the war.

The English had besieged Orléans, the key to the Loire valley, since October 1428, and hunger threatened to force its surrender. Joan of Arc, a peasant girl who said God had sent her to drive out the English, persuaded the Dauphin to send her there, and she entered the city on 29 April. Within days the revived French attacked the English forts and the siege was lifted, followed by victories along the Loire and at Patay.

The victory at Patay, where French cavalry broke the English rearguard and captured John Talbot, opened the road through English- and Burgundian-held country to Reims, the traditional coronation city. Charles was crowned there on 16 July 1429, strengthening his claim against the Treaty of Troyes. An attack on Paris in September failed, and Henry VI was crowned king of France in Paris in 1431.

Burgundian troops captured Joan at Compiègne in May 1430 and handed her to the English. At Rouen, the seat of English government in France, a church court led by Pierre Cauchon, bishop of Beauvais and an ally of the English, convicted her, and she was burned on 30 May 1431. A later church inquiry overturned the verdict about 25 years afterwards, and she became a lasting French national symbol.

England, France and Burgundy met at Arras in the summer of 1435 in what has been called Europe's first real peace congress. The English demands were seen as unrealistic, and after they left, Philip the Good of Burgundy made peace with Charles VII in the Treaty of Arras, recognising him as king. The loss of its main ally was a severe blow to England, and the treaty returned Paris to the French king.

During long truces Charles VII reorganised his army into a professional force with powerful artillery that could take castles in days. The French retook Rouen in 1449. At Formigny an English army marching to relieve Caen was attacked by the Count of Clermont and then struck in flank and rear by Arthur de Richemont. It was the last significant English field army in Normandy, and the remaining strongholds soon fell.

Charles VII turned to Gascony, England's last province; Bordeaux surrendered in 1451, but its people, largely sympathetic to the English, welcomed back an army under John Talbot in October 1452. At Castillon, Talbot attacked a French camp laid out by the artillery master Jean Bureau and was cut down by its cannon. Talbot and his son were killed in what is usually considered the last battle of the war.

The fall of Bordeaux ended English rule in Gascony and the fighting of the Hundred Years' War. England kept only Calais. No peace treaty was signed until 1475, when the Treaty of Picquigny formally ended the war, and English and later British monarchs kept the title king of France until the early nineteenth century. Defeat abroad fed the discontent that led to the Wars of the Roses in England.
